consensus_summary: Consensus identifies 'shadow of death' as the deepest gloom of mortal peril, extreme danger, or dying itself (esp. Ps 23:4, with God present), extended in prophetic/NT texts to spiritual darkness/hopelessness of humanity apart from God that Christ illuminates; philological alternative is simply 'deep darkness,' with further applications to Sheol, the deathbed, bondage, or despair.
book_summary: The symbolic Way and pattern of the world shaped like Death’s substance—sin, darkness, and bondage whose wages end at the pit or grave—explicitly opposite the Shadow of Christ (appointed times, assemblies, and humbled Way shaped like His substance that leads through death to eternal life).
consensus_core_identification: Death-associated extreme darkness/gloom experienced as mortal peril or spiritual alienation.
book_core_identification: The world’s Death-shaped symbolic way/pattern of sin, darkness, and bondage, defined as the opposite of the Shadow of Christ.
boundary_disagreement: Consensus boundaries cover lived peril, Sheol, pre-messianic spiritual darkness, or gloom without any dual ‘Shadow of Christ’ typology or identification as the ontological ‘Way/pattern of the world’; the book’s framing therefore has no shared boundary to adjust.
material_contradiction: None; the book neither denies the peril/spiritual-darkness readings nor asserts they are false, but simply supplies an unlisted core identification.
rationale: Minimum cores diverge in referent: consensus centers on an experiential or locative darkness tied to death’s threat or spiritual lostness, while the book centers on a cosmic ‘Way/pattern’ of the world modeled on Death and paired as opposite the Shadow of Christ. No primary meaning or listed alternative in the consensus responses recognizes this dual-shadow typology or ‘Death’s substance’ patterning, so the identification is absent rather than a narrowed, broadened, or contradictory version of a shared core.
strongest_objection: The entry may simply be an idiosyncratic systematization of the already-common spiritual-darkness/bondage reading (Isa 9/Luke 1 + Rom 6:23) plus Christ’s humiliation (Phil 2), rather than a genuinely new symbolic referent; traditional Psalm 23 pastoral usage is left unaddressed.
